title: How an unexpected battle for P6 in Malaysia fell apart
excerpt:
Formula 1’s midfield is so closely matched that points are hard to come by, and any top-10 finish counts as a real achievement.

So when factors such as rain throw a curve ball and create opportunities, it’s essential for those teams and their drivers to get everything right and take full advantage.

For Carlos Sainz, Alex Albon and Esteban Ocon the early stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia promised much as they made the right tyre calls and did the job on track to charge into the top eight. However, in the end, all three were to be left disappointed.

Ocon was one of the drivers who hit problems at the original start attempt, but having been given a second chance he and Haas got it right by opting for intermediates for the start as the team split its two cars. Williams also made the optimum call by putting both drivers on inters.

On the first lap it was almost like a video game for all three, as they picked their way past those ahead who had started on slicks. At the end of the lap Sainz was P6 (from 13th), Albon P7 (from 18th) and Ocon P8 (from 17th). The Haas driver was flying, and he soon made his way past both FW48s to claim P6.

At that stage – and with the slick runners falling far behind – it was looking good for all three, but the fun was not to last.

Albon was running behind Sainz when the first Safety Car sent the field into the pits for slicks, and he lost places while double-stacked behind his team mate.

At the restart Sainz was nudged into a spin at Turn 2 by Gabriel Bortoleto. With faster cars that started on slicks gaining ground under the Safety Car both Williams drivers tumbled down the order, with Albon also fighting brake problems. Sainz had to settle for P17 at the flag.

“We were having the race and doing everything right to score a point or two today,” said the Spaniard. “But then the race went away from us, obviously with the touch with Gabi taking us off. Even though I left the space, I don’t think he expected the inside of Turn 2 to be wet, and he just bumped into me.

“It was dry from there on, and it's not like our pace was amazing. Our pit stops were also not good. So it would have been a difficult day anyway.

“We would have needed to execute a perfect race, and we had two very slow pit stops. And the execution of the race from there onwards wasn't great either. I don't know if that bump from Gabi threw us off a bit as a team, but from there it was a bit scrappy, to be honest.”

To add insult to injury, Albon didn’t even see the flag due to a late gearbox problem.

“I lost out on the double stack,” he said. “We had to box early because I flat-spotted my soft tyres with the brake issue. So then it just felt like it fell away from us. The performance was nowhere, but also nowhere on my side as well.

“Unfortunately, you just want a smooth weekend, a feeling of progress, but we've had issues with parts this weekend. Not lack of parts, just performing parts, and unfortunately, if you're not on the one part that you have, you use your second best stuff, it's not good enough, and you're immediately on the back foot. And I was on the back foot massively all weekend.”

How Alonso and Aston Martin took their opportunity in Sepang

In contrast to the two Williams drivers, Ocon survived the first Safety Car period in good shape, and still in P6.

He lost a place to the flying Lewis Hamilton, but was still P7 when he made a relatively early second stop.

Others who hung on for a later stop benefited from the second Safety Car, triggered by Albon. Points thus slipped out of his hands, and he finished P15.

“We took the right tyre for the start, I decided to stay on the inter, which was the right thing,” said the Frenchman. “We had a mega first lap on the inter, I was overtaking cars. I was up to P6. It was really good. And then from the first time we boxed, we started moving rearwards.

“So we need to exactly see what happened, but we deserved more today. We had new tyres in stock. We also boxed to used tyres at the end, and we missed the last Safety Car also.

“So 100% the start of the race, 0% at the end part of the race, of success. A bit of mixed emotion, but super sad for the whole team that has worked super hard to get this car to where it was, because it was healthy, it was working well.

“We had great pace on the soft tyre in the beginning and on the inter, and we should have been fighting for the points, and we were there. So very disappointed. But it's our fault – so we'll keep working on it.”

title: Audi unpick eventful weekend amid penalty and last-lap drama
excerpt:
The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia proved to be a particularly eventful weekend for Audi, with the squad left to reflect on a “frustrating” end to Sunday’s race that saw them lose out on points during the last lap.

After progressing to Q3 in Saturday’s Qualifying, Gabriel Bortoleto lined up in P10 on the grid while team mate Nico Hulkenberg started from P15 – but both looked set for a tough start to the race when they bolted on soft tyres, a decision that quickly went against them given the still damp conditions from the heavy rainfall that had delayed the event getting underway.

Following an early stop for the intermediates, the Audis were each able to make gains. However, Bortoleto’s progress faltered when he made contact with the Williams of Carlos Sainz, an incident that the Brazilian subsequently received a 10-second time penalty for.

Hulkenberg, meanwhile, remained in the fight for points until the very end of the race and only just missed out after being overtaken by Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad on the final lap of the Grand Prix.

Furthermore, the team were handed a fine (part of which was suspended for 12 months on the condition that there is not a similar incident in that time) for an unsafe release of Hulkenberg during a pit stop.

While he had also seen a point slip away during the final stages of the race one week earlier in Azerbaijan, Hulkenberg was pragmatic about experiencing a similar fate at Sepang.

“Obviously a few times now I just missed out, but ultimately [it was] not quite good enough, our package here,” the German explained. “That's why we couldn't hang on to that point in the end, but obviously if we're honest we only got there because of some retirements and some trouble at the front.

“I feel like it was always a long shot, but I’m much happier with my performance compared to yesterday, which wasn't so difficult, but a clean race from my side. Yeah, good racing and a good afternoon.”

On the other side of the garage, Bortoleto took the blame for his collision with Sainz after what proved to be a tough afternoon in Malaysia.

“First I want to apologise to Carlos,” said Bortoleto. “I ended up touching him there and maybe destroyed his race, a bit of mine as well, created damage in my car, and after that we were just too far behind to fight for anything.

“I was racing on my own and unfortunately had another few issues through the race as well that was very difficult to manage, but anyway, I was already gone after my contact. So I apologise to him, to my team, to his team, and we move to Singapore.“

The 21-year-old still felt that there were “a lot of positives” to take forward, adding: “I think we delivered a good upgrade in Baku and it showed to be strong here. And yeah, heads up to Singapore. I'm excited for the weekend, and hopefully we can have a good one there.”

Audi’s Racing Director Allan McNish echoed that positivity, having praised the performance of the car in Malaysia whilst acknowledging that missing out on points was a frustrating end to the event.

“We got the pace of the car. That was quite clear when we got to Qualifying,” McNish reflected after the race. “I think we had got it into the right window, and Gabi delivered a really good Qualifying.

“Nico was on a similar pace till Turn 14. These things happen. And I think, we sort of got back through to roughly that point by the end of the race. Not quite that same point, but very close to it.

“So in terms of that, yeah, it was a bit frustrating to be overtaken in the last lap again, because that's two races consecutively where we've been done in the last lap and that's a little bit frustrating. But I think we know where our strengths and weaknesses are and we know we're a bit exposed, and when the Safety Car came out we become a bit more exposed.”

title: FIA Formula 2 and FIA Formula 3 announce 2027 calendars
excerpt:
The FIA Formula 2 Championship and FIA Formula 3 Championship have announced their respective calendars for the 2027 campaign.

Both junior single-seater championships will continue to support Formula 1 across the 2027 season, with F2 featuring at 14 rounds, while Formula 3 will be present at 10 rounds next year alongside both.

F2 returns to Montreal after racing in Canada for the first time in 2026, while Mexico City joins the calendar for the first time. Istanbul will also feature on the calendar as a new venue, staging a race for the first time in the FIA Formula 2 era.

Formula 3 will visit Jeddah and Montreal for the first time, while the season finale will take place at another new venue in Istanbul.

Both championships will begin their campaigns in March in Bahrain and Jeddah before heading to Melbourne in April and Montreal in May.

F2 and F3 then return to action in June around Monaco before back-to-back rounds at Silverstone and Spielberg.

Following the summer break, both championships resume racing in Monza before heading to Madrid.

F2 is the sole supporting championship in Azerbaijan in September, before both join F1 in Istanbul for what will be the season-ending F3 round.

F2 visits Mexico at the end of October before going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi for the final two rounds of the campaign.

Stefano Domenicali, President and CEO of Formula 1 said: “The 2027 FIA Formula 2 calendar will deliver another exciting season of racing across 14 rounds at some of the most iconic and challenging venues in world motorsport, including the addition of Istanbul and Mexico City.

“Formula 2 continues to play a vital role as the ultimate pathway to Formula 1, giving the most promising young drivers the opportunity to compete on the same stage as the pinnacle of our sport and showcase their talent to fans, teams and partners around the world. Year after year, the championship delivers outstanding racing and helps develop the next generation of Formula 1 stars.

"“I would like to thank the FIA President and their entire team, Bruno Michel and his team, as well as all our promoters, partners, officials, marshals and volunteers whose dedication and commitment make this Championship possible. I look forward to following another highly competitive season in 2027.”

Bruno Michel, FIA Formula 2 CEO said: “I’m very excited to add three new venues in a financially sustainable way, with the return of Montreal following its surprise addition in 2026 and the first appearance of Istanbul and Mexico City.

“We will be covering freight costs so that the territorial expansion of the calendar does not financially impact our teams.

“With a calendar spanning four continents and a carefully distributed sequence of rounds, the 2027 FIA Formula 2 Championship will offer teams and drivers a demanding and diverse season, while bringing the category to new audiences and strengthening its position as a global platform for the next generation of Formula 1 talent.”

title: 5 winners and 5 losers from the Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
Max Verstappen returned to winning ways with a beautiful drive at a rain-hit Sepang, in a race that featured plenty of overtaking. But while he and his Red Bull team celebrated, many of his rivals were left downbeat. Lawrence Barretto selects his winners and losers from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Winner: Max Verstappen

title: How McLaren got their sums wrong on Sepang tyre strategy
excerpt:
Just eight days after the team failed to score any points in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, McLaren endured another painful race day at Sepang.

It wasn’t quite as bad as Baku, but nevertheless P6 for Oscar Piastri and P9 for Lando Norris was not what the team needs or expects.

On a day when there were many strategy calls to be made, the team got the big one wrong when they opted to put both drivers on medium tyres for the start – a decision that seemed logical at the time but which was soon proved to be incorrect.

Historically Sepang is a track that dries relatively quickly, and thanks to its rough surface, puts heat into dry tyres and allows them to work even in damp conditions. That knowledge pushed McLaren and others into starting on slicks.

“At the pit wall, in terms of making calls and strategy on tyres, the most difficult moment was certainly at the start,” Team Principal Andrea Stella noted. “Where it wasn't clear [was] whether the track was requiring intermediate tyres, or it would work for the dry tyres.

“On this kind of tarmac already what we saw on the laps to the grid is that the intermediate tyres were getting damaged very rapidly, and also on this kind of tarmac, the dry tyres work very, very easily – much more easily than pretty much every other circuit.

“So it looked, from what we could observe, that the track was dry enough to stay on track with the dry tyres, and we thought that the dry tyres would have switched on pretty rapidly. But as a matter of fact, it took more laps than we thought.

“So with Lando we lost race time, and with Oscar as well, we lost race time because we needed to pit and accept that the track was only right for intermediate tyres. This was the most complicated moment.”

Piastri made a decisive call and pitted for intermediates at the end of the second formation lap, throwing away his grid position but at least putting himself on the right tyres.

The slick runners struggled so much that by the end of the first flying lap he was already back up to P10, just four spots shy of his starting position. Norris, meanwhile, had soon tumbled down to P15, and like the others still on dry tyres he lost huge chunks of time each lap.

McLaren were one of several teams where one driver pitted, and the other stuck with the slicks. However, that wasn’t a big picture choice.

“No, it wasn't as simple as splitting,” said Stella. “It was more the uncertainty as to how much it would take for the dry tyres to start to work, and as a matter of fact, it took longer than what we thought it would take.

“So ultimately, it was an incorrect judgment as to the crossover at which the dry tyres would be faster than the intermediate tyres. But there was not a logic as simple as saying, ‘Let's split, and let's see what which one is right.’ We thought that the dry tyres would switch on faster.”

Piastri admits McLaren 'need to improve' after Malaysia P6

The drivers had their input, as Stella confirmed: “I think for Oscar it was sort of Oscar himself thinking like it's not going to be rapid, and I think with Lando, it's possible that we biased Lando in the wrong direction.

“I think he was probably more in the direction that he should have pitted for inters, but as we discussed, we kind of attempted to see whether we could stay out on the medium tyres.”

By the last Safety Car, Piastri and Norris had made it up P7 and P8. George Russell’s late retirement handed the Australian a place, but Norris was wrongfooted when the Safety Car queue backed up, and he dropped to P11. After the restart he managed to gain a couple of places.

McLaren did thus at least score some points, but this was by no means a good weekend for a team that was winning races just a few weeks ago.

“We see a scenario in F1 which seems to be changing pretty rapidly,” said Stella. “In Hungary, we took some upgrades, and we were in condition to have pole position in Hungary, Zandvoort, and then we were in condition to do pole position and pretty much victory in Madrid without the Virtual Safety Car.

“And then very rapidly and interestingly, as we took upgrades as well, the picture changes. I think we have to take a look at our own development.

“We don't see any anomaly in our data, but we have to acknowledge that potentially some competitors have developed their car with bigger steps that we did.”

Stella admitted that the pecking order is hard to judge at the moment, especially after a race an outlying track like Sepang. He reserved judgement on what we might see in Singapore next weekend.

“It's a very special condition here in Malaysia,” he said. “So I think we'll have to understand better the behaviour of the cars, and also here Ferrari were very, very strong.

“I think you see that [Lewis] Hamilton was out there with Lando, and from that position he managed to recover several positions, overtaking cars through the race, meaning that it was definitely one of the best cars out there.

“I think we need to give ourselves some more time. I'm personally not in condition to say if Singapore will be now more suitable or not, because from a track layout point of view, we thought that here would be a decent circuit for us, and this because of the uncertainty caused by the new scenario from a competitiveness point of view, but also because we might have to understand a bit better the upgrades that we took ourselves. And Singapore will give us a better answer.”

title: Audi unveil special livery for Singapore GP
excerpt:
Audi have revealed a special livery for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, celebrating the city's unique identity as well as the team's first night race in Formula 1.

The R26 will sport a design that combines a Singapore-specific variant of Audi's usual Titanium Silver Grey with a traditional peranakan pattern, which will adorn the sidepods and rear wing and carry over onto Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto's race suits.

Inspired by the city's transition from daylight to twilight, the livery has been launched alongside a limited-edition Adidas capsule collection, building on 'The Art of Influence' – a 360-degree programme that brings F1 closer to fans through activations across Singapore and online.

Stefano Battiston, Chief Brand and Commercial Officer at Audi, said: “Bringing Formula 1 to the people means giving fans more ways to feel part of the team, wherever they are. Singapore shows how we can do that through one connected idea.

"Audi’s special livery expresses our brand through a design shaped by the city, and fans around the world can discover it for themselves through the online reveal.

"With the Adidas collection and experiences across Singapore, that story continues beyond the race car.

"‘The Art of Influence’ invites people to engage with the team in ways that are meaningful to them, whether they are here in the city or following from home."

title: Vasseur on how Hamilton and Leclerc saved the day at Sepang
excerpt:
Ferrari weren’t the only team to make a wrong call at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia by opting for slicks, but no one else did a better job of recovering and limiting the damage.

A race that looked to be heading for disaster after just a couple of laps ended with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc recovering for a decent outcome to finish third and fourth.

Yes, they were flattered by the late retirement of George Russell moving them both up a spot, while Isack Hadjar was hampered by a late battery issue and thus was unable to put up much of a defence.

But they did most of the work themselves with some superb driving in what was clearly a very competitive package – a performance that inevitably left Ferrari fans wondering what might have been had the right call been made at the start.

“I think 50 percent of the cars went for slicks, 50 for wets,” said Team Principal Fred Vasseur of the tyre choice. “You can't try, you just have a look on the tarmac in front of you in the pit lane, and for sure it was not the good one.

“It's not that I have no regrets – for sure, it's clear that it was better to start with inters, but we did the choice with information that we had.”

In essence the track dried more slowly than anyone expected, given past experience of Sepang.

“When you have to take your decision, you are trying to base the decision on good parameters,” said Vasseur. “But for sure, at the end of the day, we have to be lucid that it was not the right call, that it would have been much better for us to start with inters. But we were considering that it will dry very quickly, and so on. The pit stop [loss] was quite long also, 26 seconds.”

Leclerc’s race was changed when he had contact with Nico Hulkenberg at the start, and he pitted immediately for inters and a new front wing.

Several drivers who went for slicks also soon abandoned them – in some cases even before the first flying lap – but Hamilton opted to stay out, insisting that it was right to take a risk.

“We let him [have] the choice,” said Vasseur. “At the end, in this situation, they are in the car. When we are telling him that we are ready, it's just to tell him that he can pit if he thinks that it's the right call.

“He did a very good race, very smooth strategy. He was able to do a mega long stint with a very good tyre management with the soft.”

So what was the potential had the Ferraris made a different call and started on intermediates?

“I don't know, because the race is for sure different when you have to overtake 20 cars rather than run in front,” said Vasseur. “But I was not mega optimistic after Lap 1! You never know also because with dirty air, it's much more difficult, energy management and so on.

“But the pace was solid, and when Lewis was at the end of his stint with the soft, he was still doing a very good lap time.”

The race pace was certainly impressive, and ultimately that’s what propelled Hamilton and Leclerc up the order.

“We showed the same pace yesterday,” said Vasseur. “We were on the first row, but we were also on the first row in Baku. But the race pace was much better this weekend.

“It's also completely different conditions. The last two or three races we had zero [degradation]. This weekend the race was also difficult to manage for the drivers, because we did all the free practice with 60 degrees of track temp, and then you do the race with 30 degrees less, and it's another track.

“We were all a bit lost. I think when we restarted after the Safety Car, at one stage you had seven cars with soft, seven with medium, seven with hard. It's not very usual.”

So can Ferrari carry that strong form into next weekend?

“Let me have a beer tonight, and we discuss about Singapore tomorrow morning!” joked Vasseur. “It will be another one, for sure. But each one is different, and let's see.

“We were expecting to do a good performance this weekend. I think we did it. We are expecting to do also a good one next week – and I hope we'll do it.”

title: Lindblad's P10 finish 'more than we could have imagined'
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad believes his P10 finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was "more than we could have ever imagined" after starting from the back of the grid.

The Racing Bulls driver started Sunday's 55-lap race at the Sepang International Circuit in P22 and last on the grid after taking grid penalties for new engine components.

Lindblad was able to move up the field early in proceedings after starting on the intermediate tyre, as other drivers dropped away with slick tyres on the still-wet track.

A late retirement for Mercedes' George Russell and an off-track excursion for Lando Norris' McLaren behind the Safety Car ensured the 19-year-old scored his fourth points finish in succession.

"It's probably the busiest day of my F1 career and the outcome is pretty amazing. To be in the points from starting last is more than we could have ever imagined," said Lindblad, who is still in his rookie F1 season.

"I think from that side it's really good, amazing day for the team, amazing day for the whole Red Bull family, credit to Max [Verstappen] and RBPT. It's the first win for this engine, it's been absolutely amazing all year so I'm super happy for them.

"On my side, I'm not that happy with my own performance. Obviously there was some good stuff but there was a good part in the middle where I was just too slow, so I need to understand why and why I've been a little bit weaker I'd say in long runs than short runs this year.

"I've always felt good in Qualifying but the race is normally a bit more difficult, so I need to understand why that is, but super happy for the team. They've all done an absolutely perfect job, it's honestly thanks to them that we've got this performance today."

Racing Bulls enjoyed a strong day in Malaysia, as Liam Lawson finished seventh, having even battled eventual race winner Max Verstappen for third on the opening lap after an incredible launch off the grid from P11.

The result means Racing Bulls has moved 22 points clear of Alpine in their battle for P5 in the Teams' Championship, as neither Pierre Gasly or Franco Colapinto scored points in Malaysia.

"It's sort of two weekends where Alpine has been a bit quicker than us but we've managed to out-score them," said Lawson.

"I think that's really been on good decision making today on the strategy for the start. I had one of the best starts I've ever had in my career and that put us in a great position for the rest of the race."

title: Charles Leclerc voices concern after Sepang chaos: 'It was scary'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has stated that the on-track issues that occurred on the formation lap in Sepang were "scary" to endure.

Multiple cars came to a halt as they rounded the circuit at slow speed, with many others unable to accelerate due to a software bug with the power unit.

The FIA declared that a mix of factors caused this, including low engine speeds and wet weather management systems.

Leclerc revealed he was unsure what was happening behind the safety car, with Max Verstappen pulling a huge gap to the field after he got his own power back.

"At first I thought that the safety car had switched off the light, I couldn't see the safety car," Leclerc told media including RacingNews365.

"There was too much spray, so I thought the safety car had gone, and Max was taking the gap to warm up the tyres, which I was like, 'Okay, fine'.

"And then they told me on the radio, 'we think Max has a problem'. Then Max went, Lewis was slow, and I waited.

"At one point I was just like, 'okay, I'm probably just going to go'. And when I went on throttle, I had exactly the same problem.

"I realised everybody was in the same boat. We were stuck at like 20 km/h. It's a little bit scary to see that on a Formula 1 car."

Leclerc warns over major F1 shunt

Sunday's event marked the first time this year that the F1 cars were run in wet conditions in a competitive setting.

Leclerc has warned that the sport is risking a major shunt if power differences occur in low visibility.

"That's a bit our worry with these cars, not to that extent, of course, this was a problem, but whatever you have when you get out of the corner, sometimes you can have 100 horsepower more, 100 horsepower less," he said.

"You are not completely in control of the power you are given, and with this kind of visibility at the start of the race, you can have big shunts because of that.

"It's not the greatest cars to drive in these conditions."

title: McLaren admits it 'biased' Lando Norris in 'wrong direction' during F1 chaos
excerpt:
Andrea Stella has admitted McLaren may have steered Lando Norris towards the wrong tyre call during the chaotic start to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as the team misjudged when dry tyres would begin to work on a drying but still treacherous track.

Thunderstorms — and a software bug — delayed the start of the race at the Sepang International Circuit, with the field split between dry tyres and intermediates once the action eventually got underway.

Both McLarens were due to start on medium-compound Pirellis, but Oscar Piastri pitted for intermediates after the formation lap while Norris stayed out on dry rubber.

The decision cost Norris significant time, with the Briton eventually pitting, along with Piastri, for hard tyres behind the safety car at the end of lap nine, triggered by Valtteri Bottas spinning into the gravel at Turn 13.

Piastri went on to finish sixth, while Norris recovered to ninth, picking up just two points — after nearly slamming into the back of his team-mate behind the late safety car.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Stella explained that the call was complicated by how quickly the intermediate tyres were degrading on the Sepang asphalt during the laps to the grid, which suggested the dry tyre could work far sooner than it actually did.

"Well, on the pit wall, in terms of making calls on strategy and tyres, the most difficult moment was certainly at the start, when it wasn't clear whether the track was requiring intermediate tyres or if it would have worked for the dry tyres," Stella said.

"On this kind of tarmac, already what we saw on the laps to the grid is that the intermediate tyres were getting damaged very, very rapidly, and also on this kind of tarmac, the dry tyres work very, very easily, much more easily than pretty much every other circuit.

"So it looked, from what we could observe, that the track was dry enough to stay on track with the dry tyres, and we hoped that the dry tyres would have switched on pretty rapidly.

"But as a matter of fact, it took more laps than we thought. So with Lando, we lost race time, and with Oscar as well, we lost race time, because we needed to pit and accept that the track was only right for intermediate tyres. This was the most complicated moment..."

Not a deliberate split strategy

Asked whether McLaren had simply split its two cars' strategies to hedge its bets, Stella rejected that suggestion.

"It wasn't as simple as splitting [Norris and Piastri]. It was more the uncertainty as to how much it would take for the dry tyres to start to work," the McLaren team principal said.

"And, as a matter of fact, it took longer than what we thought it would take. So ultimately, it was an incorrect judgement as to the crossover at which the dry tyres would be faster than the intermediate tyres.

"But there was no logic as simple as saying, 'let's split and let's see which one is right'. We thought that the dry tyres would switch on faster."

Stella went further, suggesting Piastri had reached his own conclusion on the formation lap, while Norris had been influenced by the team's thinking.

"I think for Oscar, it was sort of Oscar himself thinking, 'it's not going to be rapid'," he added.

"And I think with Lando, it's possible that we biased Lando in the wrong direction. He was probably more in the direction that he should have pitted for inters.

"But as we discussed it, we kind of attempted to see whether we could stay out on the medium tyres."

title: The 'no fluke' secrets behind Max Verstappen and Red Bull return to F1 glory
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and Red Bull's first win of the F1 season was no fluke. RacingNews365 technical expert Paolo Filisetti explains why — and points to the upcoming acid test in Singapore.

Max Verstappen and Red Bull's victory at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was no fluke.

The RB22 proved to be an extremely competitive car around the Sepang International Circuit, helped by a series of recent upgrades.

The latest involved revisions to the upper profile of the sidepods and, most significantly, the undercut, allowing Red Bull to introduce a different aerodynamic map for the RB22 from the Spanish Grand Prix onwards.

The car is now much more precise and responsive, with Isack Hadjar's performances providing further evidence of the progress made.

It is worth remembering that, for much of the season, Verstappen had complained about the unpredictable behaviour of his car through the middle of corners, often experiencing rear-end snaps.

These reactions prevented him from having complete confidence in the RB22 and, consequently, from extracting its maximum potential.

Advantages of Sepang and the upcoming litmus test

Sepang's layout — featuring two long straights linked by the final hairpin, followed by a sequence of medium- and high-speed corners — provided an ideal opportunity to showcase the gains made with the car.

The RB22 also benefited from the powerful internal-combustion engine and excellent energy-management capabilities, although the demands placed on the power unit at Sepang ultimately proved less severe than anticipated.

Verstappen also had the advantage of being one of only three drivers to have previously won at Sepang. That prior experience, combined with his ability to interpret the circuit in light of the demands of modern F1 machinery, proved valuable both over a single lap in qualifying and in the complex management of a damp track during the race, as grip levels evolved continuously.

Now, with Singapore next on the calendar, the Marina Bay Street Circuit represents another important litmus test.

The vastly different characteristics of the circuit will reveal just how far Red Bull's development programme at Milton Keynes has transformed the RB22 — and whether the car can consistently unlock its potential across fundamentally different track layouts.

If that proves to be the case, Red Bull may finally have turned the RB22 into a genuinely all-round package.

title: Fred Vasseur finds much-needed allies as spotlight glares on Ferrari boss
excerpt:
Flavio Briatore has thrown his support behind Fred Vasseur, insisting the scrutiny faced by the Ferrari team principal is "much harder" than that endured by his rivals on the F1 grid.

Briatore's comments arrive with Vasseur in the spotlight following Ferrari's dip in form. Lewis Hamilton finishing third in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was the team's first podium in six races.

Speculation around Vasseur's future intensified further after Red Bull boss Christian Horner recently described the Ferrari team principal role as a dream job, while Italian media has reported friction between the Frenchman and CEO Benedetto Vigna over Hamilton's integration into the wider structure.

Ferrari's senior leadership, including executive chairman John Elkann and Vigna, moved to shut down the noise with an emergency press briefing last week, via chief communications officer Maria Conti, reiterating full confidence in Vasseur, who said he remains in daily contact with both men, and denying that his autonomy is restricted.

Alpine team principal Briatore, who knows what it is like to be vehemently scrutinised after the 'Crashgate' scandal of 2008 when he was in charge of Renault, said the nature of F1 coverage means questions are more pointed once results dip.

"The media look at every time you fail," said Briatore, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "It is unfortunately like that, because if you're doing well, the media is very quiet.

"The moment you're doing bad, the media wake up and [ask] 'Why?' So, we need to live with that.

"Sure, it's much harder for Fred than for us, for the number of articles, because from a media point of view the attention is very high.

"[But] We need the media because it's our business, but sometimes we need friendlier media. It's not possible, but we try."

[Article continues below]

Vasseur critique 'exaggerated'

Williams team principal James Vowles echoed that sentiment, saying the volatility of judgement aimed at whoever occupies the Maranello hot seat sets it apart from other roles on the grid.

"Obviously it's difficult," Vowles said.

"We all know, let's be frank about it, our jobs are on the line. [If] We don't do a good enough job, that puts us at risk straight away. I think that's a given. You take that when you take the title.

"But there's a difference between how you're celebrated in success and how you're punished in failure. Generally speaking, we all are.

"I would say, and this is very external when I read it, that it's exaggerated more in a way towards Fred, his predecessors in that role. I think it's much higher highs, much lower lows. That's how I see it."

title: Red Bull confirm talks to ensure F1 'complexity' does not get out of control
excerpt:
It was not a good look for F1, so the major stakeholders are now set to discuss the future.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies believes F1 was served a welcome reminder during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that the complexities of the current cars cannot be allowed to "get out of control".

Following a torrential downpour that delayed the race at the Sepang International Circuit by an initial 40 minutes, the event finally got going with a planned two formation laps behind the safety car ahead of a potential standing start.

But chaos ensued when a software bug in the standard power unit code triggered sudden and unexpected power loss across multiple cars during the formation lap.

Lewis Hamilton, Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas were among those who came to a complete halt on track before restarting their power units, with the disruption also affecting Red Bull, Audi, Haas, Cadillac, Alpine and Racing Bulls machinery.

The FIA later explained that the glitch stemmed from a safety-mandated wet-weather mode designed to cut electrical output from 350kW to 250kW.

At very low speeds, the system triggered an instant MGU-K shutdown in specific sectors, locking cars into a 60-second emergency offset that left them stranded.

Race control aborted the start procedure, and the FIA issued an emergency software patch to all competitors before the race eventually got underway.

Max Verstappen went on to win the rescheduled race, with Kimi Antonelli and Hamilton completing the podium.

[Article continues below]

Red Bull thought issue was of its own making

Mekies, speaking to select media including RacingNews365, admitted the mayhem initially looked like it was a Red Bull-specific problem before it became clear the fault was shared across the grid.

"I think it took everyone by surprise," said Mekies.

"First of all, we all felt it was an issue on our own car and power unit, and as it turned out, it was a central issue.

"It's a good reminder for all of us that we should probably make sure that complexity doesn't get out of hand and that we keep things as under control as as possible.

"I'm sure we'll have discussions with the teams, the FIA, and F1 to see how we can protect ourselves from those situations moving forward, and we make sure we keep the complexity of the cars and the systems under control."

The episode has reignited broader concerns within the paddock over the demands of the 2026 power unit rules, which shifted to a near 50-50 split between combustion and electric power and removed the MGU-H in a bid to simplify the hybrid system.

Despite that goal, the wet-weather energy control maps involved in the Sepang incident had seen minimal real-world running before the fault emerged.

The FIA has confirmed that it will undertake a thorough review of the incident that was an embarrassing look for F1.

title: Fernando Alonso sensational move rumours mounting
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has set the rumour mill in motion, with heavy speculation about a Dakar Rally tilt following his "more surprises" hint at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Fernando Alonso has been linked with a return to the Dakar Rally and possible outings in other championships after teasing "more surprises" shortly after extending his Aston Martin F1 deal into 2027.

RacingNews365 understands that some of these potential surprises are in the final stages of negotiation and that an announcement will not be long coming.

Alonso's future beyond F1 has been subject to fresh rumours after SoyMotor.com reported that the two-time drivers' champion is set to compete in the 2027 Dakar with an Aston Martin-branded Prodrive car.

The report said Alonso was due to begin testing the car imminently, with Marc Coma again tipped to sit alongside him. Nothing has been officially confirmed, however, and it was Alonso’s own comments ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that helped fuel the speculation.

Speaking to media including RacingNews365 at the Sepang International Circuit, Alonso said there could be "more surprises in the next few weeks", adding that he wanted to "find the limits of what is possible".

Dakar stands out as one of the more realistic options for 2027 because the Saudi Arabian rally takes place in January, before F1 begins its 24-race campaign in March. It would be his second appearance in the famed race, after finishing P13 in 2020, alongside the aforementioned Coma.

Driver

Fernando Alonso

Spanish

14

The other options

A return to the 24 Hours of Le Mans is similarly straightforward from a scheduling perspective. Aston Martin’s Valkyrie is already competing in the FIA World Endurance Championship and will return to Le Mans in June 2027, while F1’s Portuguese Grand Prix falls the following weekend.

Alonso won the race in 2018 and 2019 with Toyota and has previously indicated that a return, potentially through Aston Martin, remains of interest.

Formula E is a more complicated proposition. Alonso previously said the category’s new cars were appealing, but stressed that "Formula 1 is very unique and still the pinnacle of motorsport," before his full-time plans for next year were confirmed.

Formula E's 2026/27 calendar also directly clashes with F1 on several weekends, including China/Sanya, Portugal/Zandvoort, Austria/Shanghai and Belgium/Tokyo, making a full-time FE programme alongside F1 difficult to envisage in practice — and therefore unlikely, even on a race-by-race basis.

But Alonso is no stranger to trying his hand at new challenges. He has made two Indianapolis 500 starts, in 2017 and 2020, while his two Le Mans victories and 2018-19 FIA WEC title remain his standout achievements outside F1.

Max Verstappen is also continuing to explore life beyond F1, with the Red Bull driver set to race a Mercedes-AMG GT3 at Portimao on October 17, during his busy run of GT competition around the F1 calendar.

For now, though, Alonso’s next move remains speculation, and more concrete information is expected in the coming days and weeks. His "more surprises" comment has opened the door to plenty of possibilities, but as yet has not been officially confirmed.

title: George Russell facing 'double whammy' F1 penalty after 'gut-wrenching blow'
excerpt:
George Russell may be forced to take two power unit grid penalties in the coming rounds, adding further pain to the already devastating blow he suffered to his F1 title hopes by retiring from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

George Russell's retirement from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia could leave him facing two separate grid penalties for new power unit components, Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord has revealed.

Russell pulled off at the Sepang International Circuit after an undiagnosed power unit failure ended his race behind the late safety car, with just a handful of laps to go.

Running third at the time, just behind team-mate and F1 drivers' championship rival Kimi Antonelli, the Mercedes driver saw the deficit in the standings grow from a would-be 69 points to a potentially decisive 84-point hole.

"He came on the radio behind the safety car and said the power unit was starting to sound funny," Lord told media, including RacingNews365.

"We saw sensors then misbehaving, and it was clear we had to pull the car over, and we'd had a failure of some sort.

"We still need to understand what it means for his [power unit] pool, because he's not rich in low-mileage power units either, so that may mean we need to alter what had been our previous plan. But we'll understand that in more detail in the next hours."

Driver

George Russell

British

63

A costly compound effect

Mercedes had been planning to introduce its next Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) power unit specification during the Americas triple header, with Austin and Mexico City both mentioned as possible venues.

The ADUO mechanism allows manufacturers whose internal combustion engines trail the season's benchmark, which is currently Red Bull-Ford's, to earn extra in-season development tokens, and Mercedes qualified for those at both of the first two evaluation points.

But Russell's Sepang failure threatens to force Mercedes into using a fresh power unit element before that upgrade is even ready, meaning a second penalty could follow once the ADUO-specification unit arrives later in the season.

Asked if that means Russell may need to take a grid penalty earlier than planned, and before the ADUO upgrade arrives, Lord replied: "Potentially so, yeah. That's what we need to understand.

"But yes, there may be a double whammy effect there, which, for him, after such a gut-wrenching blow, and it was devastating to see him have to pull off as he did...

"Yeah, there may be a double whammy effect there that is just a really unfortunate consequence of that issue."

title: Lewis Hamilton explains why he will not visit a ‘casino’ with Ferrari
excerpt:
It was a call from the pitwall that Lewis Hamilton over-ruled.

Lewis Hamilton has joked he will not be visiting a casino any time soon with his Ferrari team after a decision made during the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Hamilton finished third at the Sepang International Circuit, behind race winner Max Verstappen in his Red Bull and Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, but only after ignoring an instruction from his Ferrari pit wall in the opening laps.

The seven-time F1 champion had started on soft tyres on a damp surface, a clear mistake as the track was still too wet for the slicks.

After being told on lap five to pit for intermediates, Hamilton refused, stating over the radio, "No, let's take the gamble", staying out until the track reached the crossover point for dry rubber, a call that proved crucial as he then scythed his way through.

Asked about overruling the call, Hamilton summed up his faith in his own judgement with a dry aside.

"Yeah, not going to go to the casino with the guys!" he said with a chuckle.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Despite the minor strategy error, Hamilton was keen to stress his confidence in the Ferrari operation moving forward, insisting he will "definitely have an open dialogue" with the team to ensure they are on the same page.

"You know, I'm really so proud of my team," he said. "The mechanics every weekend, just the work they're putting in, the engineers that accompany every weekend, the catering, everyone really, really comes and gives it their best. Their hearts are all in the right spot.

"We've definitely got areas that we need to improve and we know that, and we're not in any denial of that.

"So I think we'll have a constructive chat, we'll regroup, we'll take the positives from this weekend, and the car was really good, and we'll come back next week fighting.

"I thought there was a chance for us potentially to try and fight Max for the win, but maybe we can do that next week [in Singapore]."

title: Max Verstappen opens up on father Jos' reaction to rocky Red Bull start
excerpt:
It has been quite the journey for Max Verstappen, father Jos, and Red Bull this season.

Max Verstappen has revealed that his father Jos found the opening months of Red Bull's 2026 campaign just as difficult to watch as he found the RB22 to drive, after a dominant win in the Bahrain GP in Malaysia capped a dramatic turnaround for the team.

Verstappen controlled Sunday's race from start to finish at Sepang for his first win of the season, and 72nd of his career, giving Red Bull-Ford Powertrains its maiden success after forming its partnership.

It was a far cry from the early rounds of the season, when Verstappen's car was blighted by entry instability, mid-corner understeer and a downforce deficit that chewed through the tyres.

The handling problems left the Dutchman fighting a car that offered little steering feedback through corner entry and exit, with the new power unit seemingly compounding the balance issues.

Red Bull responded with mechanical fixes before the summer break and followed up with aerodynamic updates at Miami and Austria, before a major Baku development package addressed the remaining speed deficit through medium and high-speed corners.

Jos Verstappen, who guided his son through karting and into Formula 1, remains a regular presence in the paddock despite stepping back from day-to-day involvement.

But that closeness, built over years of working together towards the same goal, means the elder Verstappen feels every high and low of the campaign almost as intensely as his son.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Max Verstappen - 'We understand each other well'

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, after the Bahrain win, Verstappen reflected on how the struggles of the early season affected them both.

"We're all very much invested in it," said Verstappen.

"And, of course, my relationship with my dad, we really understand each other well from all the years that we have spent together working towards our goal in Formula 1.

"He's still there in the background. He's not coming to every race, but when he is there, we talk a lot about everything. He knows everything.

"And for him, I guess the beginning of the season was not nice to watch, as for me being in the car was not nice to drive."

Reflecting on the team overall and how it has performed en route to finally breaking its victory duck this season, Verstappen said: "But then seeing how the team progressed, never stopped working and really took the car and just tried to fix the issues that we had, and then deliver something like this, it's amazing.

"And the people involved, honestly, the spirit in the team is very good. Everyone is on the same line and we really understand each other well.

"So it's very enjoyable to work in the team and that's why I think everyone is super happy that we finally delivered a result like this."

title: Liam Lawson reveals Oscar Piastri wish after unexpected Max Verstappen fight
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has admitted he wishes he had fought harder against Oscar Piastri during a Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that saw him surge from P11 on the grid to briefly challenge Max Verstappen for third place.

Lawson eventually crossed the line seventh at the Sepang International Circuit, salvaging a strong result from what had looked set to be a lowly ninth-place finish, after George Russell's late retirement behind the safety car and Lando Norris' tense near-miss with Piastri just moments later reshuffled the order in the closing laps.

The Racing Bulls driver's afternoon began with a stunning opening lap, catapulting him from P11 on the grid into contention with Verstappen for the final podium spot inside the first corner.

Although that fight did not last, the 24-year-old's pace through the second stint kept him firmly in the mix as the race unfolded over its 55 laps.

Asked about his brilliant start, Lawson told media, including RacingNews365, that he had not anticipated such an immediate opportunity.

"Great start," the New Zealander said. "I didn't expect to be fighting Max in Turn 1 from where I was starting, but the car hooked up, and yeah, just very, very happy, very proud of the team.

"All the right decisions today with tyre choices, as much as sometimes I doubted it, to be honest. But I think we had quite a good car as well. Especially that second stint was very strong for us."

Lawson rues Piastri scrap

Lawson's afternoon also included a tussle with Piastri, whom he fought in Turn 1 before easing off the defence into Turn 4, a decision he later felt left points on the table.

Asked whether he could have secured an even better result, Lawson reflected on how the race had looked from inside the cockpit before fortune turned in his favour, saying: "No, that's the thing.

"There was a point in the race where I thought, 'I feel like we've done a lot here all for a P9', and then we obviously got very lucky at the end there.

"And to be honest, I kind of wish I'd fought Oscar more because I passed them in Turn 1, and then I didn't really defend too hard into 4; I just braked a bit early because I expected them to be quite a bit quicker, and they didn't really drive away that much. But happy with the P7."

title: Sergio Perez airs stern criticism after 'rental go-kart' chaos: 'Unacceptable'
excerpt:

Sergio Perez has hit out at the "totally unacceptable" issues that occurred on the formation lap at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Multiple cars came to a halt while many others were without significant power, which came due to a software bug in the power units.

The issue caused another long delay to the start of the race, which had already been postponed due to adverse weather conditions.

Amid a series of complaints this year from the drivers regarding the new power units, Sunday's display gave them more ammunition.

While some drivers were more reserved, as they did not want to berate the sport further, Perez did not hold back.

"It felt like you were in a rental [go-]kart and you ran out of time," Perez told media including RacingNews365.

"It's obviously not great what happened. I'm sure we will learn from it as a sport, but what happened is totally unacceptable for the sport."

Driver

Sergio Pérez

Mexican

11

"I thought it was going to be dry, because when I did the laps to get to the grid, the formation laps, the first one, it was raining," he said.

title: F2 and F3 unveil 2027 calendars racing across four continents
excerpt:
Formula 2 has confirmed its 2027 calendar, with 14 rounds spanning Asia, Oceania, Europe and the Americas.

Istanbul and Mexico City join the schedule as new venues, both staged in October, while Montreal returns following its addition to the 2026 campaign.

The season opens in Sakhir in March alongside Formula 1, before a direct trip to Jeddah a week later. The field then heads to Melbourne and on to Montreal.

The European leg begins at Monte-Carlo in June, followed by a Silverstone and Spielberg double-header in July ahead of the summer break. September brings three rounds in succession: Monza, Madrid and Baku.

October sees F2 race at Istanbul for the first time, at the demanding circuit returning to the F1 calendar, before heading to Mexico City for another new addition. The season closes with back-to-back finales in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in December.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said the calendar "reflects the continued strength and global growth of an important championship at the heart of our driver development pathway."

He added: "The addition of Istanbul and Mexico City will bring Formula 2 to new audiences and give the next generation of talent the opportunity to compete on an even greater variety of circuits around the world."

Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said the calendar "will deliver another exciting season of racing across 14 rounds at some of the most iconic and challenging venues in world motorsport."

"Formula 2 continues to play a vital role as the ultimate pathway to Formula 1," he said.

F3 has also unveiled its calendar and will race in 10 rounds, from Bahrain and Jeddah in March, through to Turkey in early October, taking in Melbourne, Montreal, Monaco, Silverstone, Austria, Monza and Madrid along the way.

title: Will Max Verstappen beat Michael Schumacher's grand prix victory tally?
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's victory in the Bahrain GP in Malaysia on Sunday took him to 72 F1 grand prix wins, moving the Red Bull driver to within 19 of Michael Schumacher's total of 91.

But can Verstappen eventually overhaul the seven-time F1 champion? Only Lewis Hamilton, with 106 wins, stands above the duo.

The raw numbers favour Verstappen heavily on one measure. By the age of 28, he has already more than doubled Schumacher's win count at the same age, a gap largely explained by Verstappen's earlier F1 debut and the sport's expanded modern calendars, which now offer far more races per season than Schumacher had available.

But starts-for-starts, the picture shifts. Across equivalent numbers of race starts, Schumacher's win total and victory percentage remain higher than Verstappen's at the same stage of his career, a reminder that Ferrari's early-2000s dominance was built on a smaller but relentlessly efficient points-scoring machine.

Verstappen's extended Red Bull contract, running through 2030, gives him a potential runway of at least four more full seasons to close the gap, assuming the team can maintain competitiveness through the new technical regulations.

After breaking its win drought in Sepang, can Red Bull build on that and keep delivering winning machinery into next year and beyond, one that will shape Verstappen's realistic chances of reaching 91 wins, let alone surpassing them, before his contract expires?

title: 'F1 drivers in uproar' with 'Red Bull running out of excuses to sack Liam Lawson' - International Media Reacts
excerpt:
Find out how the world's media reacted to the 2026 F1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, at the Sepang International Circuit!

Max Verstappen finally returned to the top step of the podium at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as the Red Bull driver overcame a rain-delayed start, an early loss of power and an opening-lap deficit to the Mercedes cars to claim his first victory of the season.

Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton completed the top three at the Sepang International Circuit, with the latter producing one of the drives of his Ferrari career, recovering from 18th place after an ill-fated slick-tyre gamble.

The race itself provided an extraordinary amount of drama before the lights had even gone out. Heavy rain delayed the start, while several cars subsequently suffered power-related problems during the formation laps, forcing the FIA to suspend the starting procedure for a further period and leaving the grid in confusion.

Once racing finally got under way, changing conditions, safety car interventions and a late George Russell retirement produced a chaotic afternoon at Sepang.

Verstappen's victory was also a significant milestone for Red Bull Ford Powertrains, delivering the new power-unit project its first Formula 1 win.

Antonelli's second place further strengthened his championship position, while Hamilton's unlikely podium provided a remarkable recovery from what initially looked like a disastrous Ferrari strategy call.

Here's how international media reacted to a remarkable Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the 16th round of the F1 season.

🇬🇧 The Telegraph – F1 drivers in uproar as 'software glitch' creates Bahrain GP chaos

The Telegraph focuses on the extraordinary scenes before the Bahrain Grand Prix, arguing that Formula 1 suffered one of its most embarrassing moments in decades.

Heavy rain initially delayed the race, but the situation became farcical when several of the sport's technologically advanced cars struggled to operate properly while circulating slowly behind the safety car.

The problem appeared to stem from the complexity of the 2026 power units, with low engine speeds and wet-weather energy management causing cars to lose power and forcing the FIA to suspend the start.

The Telegraph argues that the incident raises serious questions about whether F1's increasingly complicated machinery has become too sophisticated for its own good, particularly if a relatively ordinary spell of rain can prevent the cars from racing.

🇳🇱 De Telegraaf – Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies promises aggressive approach and thanks late Dietrich Mateschitz: 'The whole world had said no to this project'

De Telegraaf focuses on Laurent Mekies' determination to preserve Red Bull's famously aggressive competitive mentality as the team moves into a new era.

The Red Bull team principal has made clear that the organisation will continue to push the limits, while also paying tribute to the late Dietrich Mateschitz and the vision that led to Red Bull entering Formula 1 in the first place.

The article places particular emphasis on the significance of the team's new Red Bull Ford Powertrains project, which had been viewed with considerable scepticism before finally delivering its maiden victory at Sepang.

Verstappen's win therefore represents more than an important result for the Dutchman – it is validation for a project that, as Mekies notes, many people once believed would never work.

🇮🇹 Gazzetta dello Sport – After 300 days, Mad Max is back: from thoughts of retirement to 'peace' with Formula 1

Gazzetta dello Sport views Verstappen's Sepang victory as a potential turning point in his difficult relationship with Formula 1's new generation of cars.

The Italian outlet highlights the more than 300-day wait for the Dutchman to return to the top step, during which Verstappen had openly questioned whether the new regulations and driving characteristics were compatible with his vision of F1.

His victory at Sepang – the circuit where he last won in 2017 – offered a welcome reminder of what he can produce when Red Bull gives him a competitive car.

Gazzetta also underlines the significance of Verstappen winning with Red Bull's new Ford-powered unit, suggesting the triumph could help repair some of the frustration that had fuelled speculation over his long-term future in the sport

🇫🇷 L'Équipe – 'Everyone managed to overtake me in the opening laps': from second on the grid to 18th before a fantastic comeback to the podium, Hamilton did more than limit the damage

L'Équipe concentrates on Hamilton's extraordinary recovery drive after his race appeared to unravel almost immediately.

The Ferrari driver started second but slipped as low as 18th after struggling with the wet conditions and Ferrari's decision to put him on slick tyres before the circuit was ready for them.

Rather than allowing the mistake to ruin his afternoon, Hamilton steadily worked his way back through the field as the track dried, eventually recovering to third and completing a remarkable turnaround.

L'Équipe therefore argues that Hamilton did far more than simply 'limit the damage', with his experience and overtaking ability proving decisive in turning a potential disaster into a podium finish.

🇳🇿 NZ Herald – Why Red Bull are running out of excuses to sack Liam Lawson

The NZ Herald takes a much more critical view of Liam Lawson, questioning whether Red Bull can continue to justify retaining the New Zealander despite the team's willingness to give him opportunities.

The opinion piece argues that Lawson's position is becoming increasingly difficult to defend when compared with the expectations placed on Red Bull's second driver and the depth of talent available elsewhere within the organisation.

Rather than treating the difficulties as solely the result of bad luck or an imperfect car, the article questions whether Lawson is doing enough to convince Red Bull that he deserves his place.

The piece consequently puts pressure on the Kiwi ahead of the next stage of the season, suggesting that Red Bull's patience cannot last indefinitely.

🇦🇺 Herald Sun – 'Absolute disgrace': F1 launches review after drivers blast 'computer cars' chaos at Bahrain GP

The Herald Sun focuses on the fallout from the bizarre formation-lap problems, with Formula 1 and the FIA facing an investigation after multiple cars suffered power-related failures in the wet.

Drivers were openly critical of the situation, with the complexity of the 2026 power units coming under intense scrutiny after cars struggled simply to circulate behind the safety car.

The FIA has subsequently committed to a full review, acknowledging that the combination of low engine speeds, low grip and wet-weather energy-management settings had produced an unintended loss of power that had not been detected during testing.

The Herald Sun presents the episode as a major embarrassment for F1, particularly given the sport's claims to represent the pinnacle of automotive technology.
